one_liner: Three small CUDA GEMV kernels (fp16, int8, int4 weights x fp16 vector) beating 2023 PyTorch fp16 matmul by 1.1-2.7x.
what_it_does: Computes y = A x for a row-major n x n matrix and an n-element fp16 vector on NVIDIA GPUs, with three kernels: gemv_fp16, gemv_quantized_int8 and gemv_quantized_int4 (int8/int4 weights dequantized on the fly with one per-tensor fp16 scale and zero point). Each is a plain __global__ function taking device pointers, the length n and num_per_thread; the caller picks blockDim (x threads per row, y rows per block) and launches grid (1, n / blockDim.y). There is no library wrapper, batching or stream handling; the repo is a benchmark program (./gemv) plus a PyTorch baseline script.
how_it_is_fast: GEMV is memory-bound, so the kernels aim at DRAM bandwidth: p = blockDim.x threads share one row, each loading 16 bytes at a time (float4 holding 8 halves; half4 holding 8 int8 values; two 4-byte packs of 8 int4 values each), and multiply in fp32 registers. Partial sums are combined with a __shfl_down_sync warp reduction (CUTLASS-style), plus one shared-memory pass when a row uses more than 32 threads. Block shape is hand-tuned per size and GPU; on the 3090 at n=16384 the fp16 kernel reaches an estimated 881.8 GB/s of 936 GB/s versus 776.3 GB/s for PyTorch.
when_to_use: Batch-1 matrix-vector products on fp16 weights (LLM-decode-style GEMV) on Pascal or consumer Ampere GPUs, where you can hand-pick blockDim per matrix size.
Weight-only int8 or int4 GEMV with a single per-tensor scale/zero point, when you want the bandwidth saving of quantized weights in a kernel small enough to read in a few minutes.
Power-of-two sizes from 512 to 16384, the only range the authors measured.
As a teaching example of vectorized loads plus warp-shuffle reduction for memory-bound kernels.
when_not_to_use: Modern data-center GPUs without re-measuring: issue #3 (open) reports the fp16 kernel slower than PyTorch on an A30 (8550.95 ms vs 6031.96 ms for 10,000 iterations at n=16384, about 0.71x, derived from page data).
Real quantized LLM weights: only one per-tensor scale and zero point is supported (no per-channel or group-wise scales), and int4 values are unsigned 0..15.
Batch sizes above 1 (GEMM), non-power-of-two or non-square shapes: the README and harness assume square power-of-two sizes, and issue #6 asking about rectangular matrices has no answer.
Small fp16 matrices on newer cards when the gain matters: on the 3090 the fp16 speedup is 1.02x at n=8192 and 1.13x at n=2048 (derived from page data).
Long-lived production use: no commits since 2023-06-06 and no releases.

integration.dependencies: CUDA runtime and cuda_fp16; curand only for the test data generator; PyTorch only for baseline.py; Nsight Systems for the published timings
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 nvcc; README lists CUDA 11.7 and Nsight Systems 2023.1.2; Makefile builds SASS for sm_60, sm_70, sm_75 and sm_86 only
integration.platforms: NVIDIA GPUs; measured on P100 and RTX 3090 (README says 3090 Ti); other architectures such as sm_80/sm_89/sm_90 need a Makefile -gencode edit because no PTX fallback is emitted
integration.thread_safety: not documented (stateless kernels; launches are the caller's responsibility)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: false - raw __global__ kernels with caller-chosen launch geometry, not a torch.matmul or cublasGemv replacement

gotchas: Launch geometry is the caller's job and is not bounds-checked: rows are not guarded, so n must be divisible by blockDim.y; n / blockDim.x must be at least 8 (fp16/int8) or 16 (int4); blockDim.y must be at most 64 (shared-memory array size); and n must be a multiple of 8 for the 16-byte loads.
Best blockDim differs by size and GPU (for example n=4096 uses 128x8 on the P100 but 256x1 on the 3090), so the published speedups need the same per-size tuning.
The harness's correctness kernels only print mismatches and never fail the run; the fp16 tolerance is an absolute 0.125 * n / 512 (4.0 at n=16384).
The int8/int4 timings move 2x/4x fewer matrix bytes than the fp16 PyTorch baseline, so their 'speedups' are not like-for-like; PyTorch had no direct quantized GEMV to compare against.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick FastGEMV over Marlin or BitBLAS when you want a tiny fp16 or per-tensor int8/int4 GEMV you can read and adapt; Marlin and BitBLAS support group-wise quantization, batch sizes above 1 and newer GPUs, and are measured against current baselines. fast.cu and bare-metal target compute-bound GEMM, not matrix-vector work.
verified_claims_summary: Nsight Systems kernel-time averages (10,000 iterations) for an n x n fp16 matrix times an n x 1 fp16 vector, against torch.matmul of mid-2023 (PyTorch version not stated; nvcc -O3, CUDA 11.7): 1.44-2.70x faster on a P100 (peak at n=8192, where PyTorch dropped to 202 GB/s) and 1.02-1.40x faster on an RTX 3090 (4372.4 vs 6106.2 ns at n=1024, 609235 vs 691660.6 ns at n=16384). One independent user report (issue #3, A30, CUDA 12.2, PyTorch 2.1) found the fp16 kernel slower than PyTorch at n=16384.
status_note: Abandoned since 2023-06-06 (130 stars, MIT, four open issues without maintainer replies), but the kernels are a few hundred lines and easy to vendor and retune.
